Choose a cell count from the elbow of the k-means WSS curve

Source: R/level-selection.R
determine_optimal_levels.Rd

Fits k-means to the coordinates at \(k = 1\) to max_levels cells and returns the count at the elbow of the within-cluster sum of squares (WSS), read on log-log axes, with its two neighbours. Points with no cluster structure have no elbow, and the result is then NA with a warning. For a count chosen from the response, use resolution_profile().

Usage

determine_optimal_levels(
  data_sf,
  max_levels = 12L,
  top_n = 3L,
  sample_n = 1500L,
  set_seed = 123L,
  response_var = NULL,
  predictor_vars = NULL,
  criterion = c("geometric", "morans_i", "combined"),
  select_on = c("all", "split"),
  on_no_elbow = c("na", "warn", "error")
)

Arguments

data_sf

An sf object. Non-point geometries are reduced to points with coerce_to_points(). Features without a location are dropped with a warning, and a layer that mixes XY and XYZ geometries or carries M is read in x and y (see spatialkit-geometry).

max_levels

Integer upper bound on levels. Default 12. The sweep also stops at the number of distinct locations (k-means cannot place more centres) and one short of the number of points.

top_n

Integer; how many candidates to return. Default 3. Under criterion = "geometric" the candidate set is the elbow and its two immediate neighbours, so at most 3 values are returned however large top_n is; only the model-aware criteria can return more. Under those it also sets the counts scored, the elbow plus or minus max(4, top_n): a top_n above 4 scores more counts, and under "morans_i" one of them can rank first. A count scores the same whichever top_n puts it in the window.

sample_n

Integer; subsample size for speed. Default 1500.

set_seed

Integer RNG seed for the subsample and the k-means++ restarts; restored afterwards. Default 123. The rows are put in coordinate order before either, so the answer does not depend on the order they come in.

response_var

Name of the response column (numeric or logical), or NULL. Read under criterion = "morans_i", which ranks the counts around the elbow by Moran's I of the cell means, and "combined", which reports that statistic beside the elbow's ranking; under "geometric", the default, it is not read. Logicals are read as 0/1; a factor or character response raises an error and is never coerced, because the residuals of an OLS fit to arbitrary level codes carry no meaning to test for autocorrelation. Rows where it, or a predictor, is missing or non-finite stay in the WSS sweep and the cells and are left out of Moran's I; a logged warning gives their number.

predictor_vars

Optional predictor column names, read where response_var is. Must be numeric or logical (logicals are read as 0/1); factor/character columns raise an error. Without them the model-aware criteria regress the cell means on an intercept alone, as resolution_profile() does.

criterion

One of "geometric" (default: the elbow and its two neighbours, read off the coordinates alone), "morans_i" (among the candidates around the elbow, the \(k\) at which Moran's I of the cell means, or of their regression residuals, is least significant: the count at which neighbouring cells stop resembling each other, which need not be the count that represents the response best), or "combined" (the candidates around the elbow in the order of the WSS curve's log-log sag, the quantity the elbow is read from, with Moran's I of the cell means and its \(z\) in the diagnostics; the statistic does not take part in the ranking). Under "morans_i" a warning of class spatialkit_diagnostic_ranking says that the ranking is by a diagnostic of the cell means; its condition carries k (the count ranked first), criterion, first_computable (the first count at which the statistic is finite) and window (the first and last count tried). "morans_i" and "combined" fall back to "geometric", with a warning, when response_var is not given, and with a logged warning when no candidate clears the nine-cell floor described under "Model-aware criteria". A response_var or predictor_vars naming a column that is not in data_sf is an error under every criterion. Supplying both response_var and predictor_vars does not change the criterion: under "geometric" neither is read, and a line logged at the INFO level says that "combined" reports Moran's I.

select_on

"all" (default) selects on every point; "split" reads the response on one spatially blocked half of the points only and returns the other half as the set to estimate on, so that the standard errors computed downstream on the chosen cells are not post-selection. The count is still chosen for the whole layer. See "Post-selection inference".

on_no_elbow

What to do when the count is not a finding about the data: the WSS curve has no elbow, the ladder is too short to show one, or there are too few points or locations for a ladder at all. Each choice raises a condition of class spatialkit_no_elbow there, which carries k (the count the chord rule or the ladder gives), sag (the largest log-log sag of the curve; an elbow needs \(\log 1.25\)) and structured = FALSE, so a caller can catch it without matching the message. "na" (default) returns NA_integer_ there, with a warning of that class, and every result under "na" carries the attributes structured (TRUE when the WSS curve has an elbow, FALSE with the NA) and sag, so one test of attr(k, "structured") covers both outcomes. "warn" returns the counts the chord rule or the ladder gives (see Value), with the same warning; its results carry neither attribute. "error" stops with an error of that class. Under the model-aware criteria the candidates are scored around the elbow: with no elbow, "na" and "error" score none, and under "warn" the ladder places that window.

Value

An integer vector of candidate counts, best first:

"geometric"

The elbow, then its lower and upper neighbours.

"morans_i"

The candidates in the order of \(|z|\), with a warning of class spatialkit_diagnostic_ranking.

"combined"

The candidates around the elbow in the order of the sag.

No elbow

NA_integer_, with a warning of class spatialkit_no_elbow; under on_no_elbow = "warn", the ladder's choice and its neighbours, with the same warning. So it is when the ladder is too short to show an elbow (max_levels of 1 or 2), and for a layer with fewer than three points or every point on one location, which has no ladder (1 under "warn"). A layer with no points is an error.

k[1] is the top-ranked count, or NA, on every path, and top_n = 1 returns it alone. The vector can carry these attributes:

structured, sag

Under the default on_no_elbow = "na", on every result: structured is TRUE when the WSS curve has an elbow and FALSE with the NA, and sag is the curve's largest log-log sag. None under "warn" or "error". The geometric path carries no other attribute.

diagnostics

Under "morans_i" and "combined": a list with per-\(k\) Moran's I (moran_i) and standardised deviates (moran_z), the WSS curve (wss) with the relative between-restart spread at each \(k\) (wss_spread), the number of rising steps on it (wss_bumps), the restart budget (nstart), the elbow the scored neighbourhood was drawn around (knee_k), whether the WSS curve has an elbow (structured) and its largest log-log sag (sag), the \(k\) at which k-means failed (failed_k; their wss entries are interpolated from the neighbours, not measured) and the \(k\) the model-aware pass scored (eval_ks, the elbow's neighbourhood). Under "combined" it also carries the WSS of the re-run clustering at those \(k\) (wss_eval, the clustering Moran's I is computed on; reported, not ranked on), the rank of the sag of wss that ordered them (combined_rank, named by \(k\); with no elbow every candidate ties and the order is by distance from knee_k) and criterion = "combined". When "combined" returned the geometric ranking because the elbow is below ten cells, it carries criterion = "geometric" and fallback (the reason) in place of combined_rank. The NA the default returns on a model-aware call whose WSS curve has no elbow (or a ladder too short to show one) carries the attribute too, with what the sweep measured: moran_i and moran_z all NA and eval_ks empty, since no count was scored, knee_k the count the chord rule lands on, and structured = FALSE. Under "combined", Moran's I computable at no candidate of a neighbourhood that reaches ten cells leaves the attribute in place, with moran_i and moran_z all NA, and a logged warning says so. The attribute is absent when the model-aware path falls back to the geometric result (no viable \(k\) in the elbow's neighbourhood, a neighbourhood that ends at nine cells or fewer, or, under "morans_i", Moran's I computable at no candidate); these fallbacks are logged as warnings. It is absent too on the NA of a layer with no ladder (fewer than three points, one location, or k-means failing at every \(k\) from 2).

split

With select_on = "split", on every path: a list with selection and estimation (integer row positions in data_sf), method and seed.

A rising WSS curve is logged on every path. For a per-level table of criteria, cell support, restart spread and the flat region, see resolution_profile().

How the elbow is read

Points with no cluster structure have a WSS curve close to \(c/k\). The classical rule, the point furthest below the chord from the first to the last \(k\), still finds a "knee" on such a curve on linear axes, at about \(\sqrt{K_{max}}\): 4 at the default max_levels = 12 and 13 at 160, whatever the data. On \(\log k\) against \(\log\) WSS that curve is a straight line, while separated clusters fall faster than it until there is one cell per cluster and like it after, a bend at the cluster count. The elbow is therefore the \(k\) whose \(\log\) WSS sags furthest below the straight line joining \(k = 1\) and \(K_{max}\) on those axes, and it counts as one only when the sag is at least \(\log 1.25\) (the WSS a fifth below the power law through the ends).

An elongated extent also bends, at about its aspect ratio, because the first cuts go across its long axis; past the threshold that bend is reported as an elbow, and it describes the shape of the extent rather than clusters in it. When locations repeat (stations visited many times), the sweep can reach one cell per distinct location, where the WSS is zero (to within \(10^{-12}\) of the total). That \(k\) has no place on log axes and is left out of the line, but the fall to zero is the sharpest bend there is: when the rest of the curve has no elbow, the number of distinct locations is the elbow.

When there is no elbow

With no elbow the function returns NA, so that a count which is not a finding is not passed on as one. The result carries structured = FALSE and the largest sag as sag, and a warning of class spatialkit_no_elbow says why. The count the linear-axis rule gives there is the ladder's and not the data's: about \(\sqrt{K_{max}}\), 3 or 4 cells at the default, close to one mean for the whole layer. The warning carries it as k and the largest sag as sag. on_no_elbow = "warn" returns that count all the same, with the same warning, and "error" stops.

Model-aware criteria

Under criterion = "morans_i" or "combined", with a response_var, the elbow is supplemented with Moran's I of the cell means at each candidate \(k\): the cell means are regressed on the cell-mean predictors (on an intercept alone when no predictor_vars are given) and Moran's I is computed on the residuals over each cell's 8 nearest cells. Under "geometric", the default, response_var and predictor_vars are not read, whether one or both are given.

Moran's I of the cell means tests whether neighbouring cells are independent. It does not measure the autocorrelation the cells leave unexplained in the response, and it does not say how well they represent it: on an autocorrelated response it grows as the cells get finer than the range, because neighbouring cells then resemble each other, and it is close to 0 at about 10 to 20 cells whatever the data, where the neighbour graph is nearly complete.

"morans_i" prefers the candidate with the smallest \(|z|\): the count at which neighbouring cell means stop resembling each other, cells about as wide as the range. Only the elbow's neighbourhood is scored, so the response moves the answer by at most a few cells either side of the elbow. That ranking is by a diagnostic of the cell means and not by a count rule, and it is returned with a warning of class spatialkit_diagnostic_ranking that says so and gives the count ranked first, the first count the statistic could be computed at and the counts scored. select_resolution() refuses the same statistic unless asked with diagnostic = TRUE; here the criterion is asked for by name, so the count is returned and the warning carries the caveat.

"morans_i" ranks on the standardised deviate \(|z| = |I - E[I]| / \mathrm{sd}(I)\), using the Cliff and Ord regression residual moments, and not on \(|I|\): both \(E[I]\) and \(Var[I]\) depend on the number of cells, so \(|I|\) falls as \(k\) grows whether or not the finer cells capture anything, and a ranking by \(|I|\) would prefer the largest candidate for arithmetic reasons alone. The cell-level residuals are OLS residuals by construction, which is the case those moments are derived for, but the derivation also assumes errors of equal variance, and a cell mean over \(n_j\) points has a variance proportional to \(1/n_j\), so \(z\) is less reliable where single-point cells sit next to cells of many points. Where structure remains, \(|z|\) mixes its size with the number of cells it is measured on, since \(\mathrm{sd}(I)\) shrinks as cells are added. Both quantities are reported in the "diagnostics" attribute, as moran_i and moran_z.

Moran's I is computed with an 8-nearest-neighbour weight matrix, so it carries information only once there are more than nine cells. At nine or fewer, every cell is a neighbour of every other, the row-standardised weight matrix is complete, and Moran's I is exactly \(-1/(k - 1)\) for any residual vector. The residual moments then give \(E[I] = I\) and \(\mathrm{Var}[I] = 0\), so the standardised deviate is \(0/0\): those candidates return NA and are left out of the ranking of "morans_i". When no candidate in the elbow's neighbourhood clears the floor, the call falls back to the geometric ranking and logs a warning that says so. On points with no cluster structure the elbow sits near \(\sqrt{K_{max}}\) and the neighbourhood is the elbow plus or minus max(4, top_n), so the neighbourhood reaches ten cells only from about max_levels = 40. On such a layer resolution_profile(), which scores Moran's z at every level of its ladder, is the model-aware view.

"combined" is the elbow's ranking of the counts around it, best sag first, with Moran's I of the cell means and its \(z\) beside it in the diagnostics; Moran's I does not take part in the ranking, and the result is not an estimate of the number of clusters. The sag is read off the sweep's WSS curve, the one the elbow is read from, so with an elbow the first count is the elbow and the counts after it come in order of sag; they can differ from the two neighbours "geometric" returns. An elbow below ten cells is a count Moran's I cannot score: the geometric ranking is returned, the elbow and its two neighbours, with a logged warning, and the diagnostics record it (see Value). When the WSS curve has no elbow (under on_no_elbow = "warn") the sag is flat, every candidate tied, and the window comes out in order of distance from the count the chord rule lands on, which is the geometric order. The k-means re-run at each candidate, whose cells Moran's I is computed on, can land in another optimum than the sweep; its WSS is reported as wss_eval and does not rank. Where Moran's I can be computed at no candidate of a window that reaches ten cells (a constant response, too few cells holding a row with one, or too few in the half that select_on = "split" reads), moran_i and moran_z are NA, the log gives the reason at the WARN level, and the counts are ranked as they would be otherwise.

Use "geometric" when the cell count should follow the clustering of the points, "morans_i" for a ranking by the diagnostic, and resolution_profile() when the response should drive the count.

The k-means sweep

The WSS curve is read for its shape, so it is fitted to be smooth. Every point on it is a k-means local optimum, and with a few random restarts the curve mixes level effects with optimisation noise and can rise from one \(k\) to the next. Each \(k\) is therefore fitted as the best of 25 restarts seeded by k-means++ (Arthur and Vassilvitskii 2007). A fixed budget of restarts follows Fränti and Sieranoja (2019), and Steinley (2003) shows why the usual handful is not enough; 25 is the package's choice, not a published figure. A curve that still rises somewhere is reported and not refused. A logged warning names the number of rising steps, and the model-aware paths return it as wss_bumps in the "diagnostics" attribute beside wss_spread, the relative spread of WSS across the restarts at each \(k\).

The sweep is plain k-means, whatever the cells are built with afterwards. This function has no partition argument: the elbow is a reading of the sum of squares that plain k-means minimises, and the cells behind Moran's z are that partition's. A count returned here says nothing about density-weighted cells; resolution_profile(), whose cells are of that kind by default, scores counts of those.

To keep memory use and run time bounded for large max_levels, the sweep records only the WSS at each \(k\), without the cluster assignments. Moran's I is then evaluated on demand: k-means is re-run only for a neighbourhood around the elbow (plus or minus 4 by default, or plus or minus top_n if larger). The re-run at each count draws its starts from a stream of its own, seeded before the sweep, so for one set_seed a count gets the same cells, wss_eval and Moran's I in any neighbourhood that holds it, whichever top_n and max_levels set the neighbourhood: a larger top_n adds counts to the neighbourhood and leaves the scores of the others as they were.

Post-selection inference

When the selection reads the response (here, under criterion = "morans_i" with a response), everything estimated afterwards on the chosen cells is estimated on data that already influenced the choice, and its standard errors are post-selection ones: descriptive, not at nominal coverage (Gao, Bien and Witten 2022; Chen and Witten 2023 give the exact selective test for two k-means clusters, the first link of this chain). The exposure is narrower than "the partition was chosen on the response": every partition here is k-means on the coordinates alone, and the response only decides which count is ranked first. It is not zero, because the count determines every cell the downstream standard errors are computed over. Under "combined" the response reaches the diagnostics and not the ranking, which is the same whether or not Moran's I can be computed.

select_on = "split" is sample splitting: the layer is cut into two spatially blocked halves (make_folds(k = 2, method = "block_kfold")), the criteria that read the response (Moran's I on the cell means) read the first half only, and the row positions of both halves come back in the "split" attribute (selection and estimation). The WSS curve and the k-means cells still use every point: they read coordinates alone, and the count is for a tessellation of every point, so it is chosen on that layer's extent and clusters rather than on half of them. Build the tessellation on every point (cells are geometry), but aggregate and fit on data_sf[attr(x, "split")$estimation, ], whose response the selection never saw. That keeps the selection's use of the response out of the estimates, but only as far as the two halves are independent: the split has no buffer, so points near the border between them are correlated with the selection half over the autocorrelation range, and coverage is nominal only when that range is short against the blocks. The price is precision: half the points estimate, and García Rasines and Young (2023) show a contiguous spatial half is less efficient than the exchangeable split the i.i.d. theory assumes, because the two halves are not interchangeable. Two alternatives keep the whole sample: data thinning for count responses (Neufeld et al. 2024) and data fission for Gaussian-like ones (Leiner et al. 2023). Neither is implemented here; the split needs no distributional assumption. Under "combined" the split changes only the rows the diagnostics read. Selection on coordinates alone ("geometric", whatever variables are given) is not exposed in this way, and "split" then changes nothing but the attribute.

The estimation rows cover only the estimation half's blocks, while the cells cover the whole layer, so the estimation rows do not fill every cell. A cell inside the selection half gets none and comes back NA; a cell across the border between the halves is estimated from its estimation-half points alone, and its standard error describes that part, not the cell. Count, per cell, how many of its points are estimation rows, and read inferential results only off cells whose points all are.

References

Arthur, D. and Vassilvitskii, S. (2007). k-means++: the advantages of careful seeding. Proceedings of the 18th Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms, 1027–1035.

Fränti, P. and Sieranoja, S. (2019). How much can k-means be improved by using better initialization and repeats? Pattern Recognition, 93, 95–112. doi:10.1016/j.patcog.2019.04.014

Steinley, D. (2003). Local optima in K-means clustering: what you don't know may hurt you. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 294–304. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.294

Gao, L. L., Bien, J. and Witten, D. (2022). Selective inference for hierarchical clustering. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 119, 332–342. doi:10.1080/01621459.2022.2116331

Chen, Y. T. and Witten, D. M. (2023). Selective inference for k-means clustering. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 24(152), 1–41. https://jmlr.org/papers/v24/22-0371.html

García Rasines, D. and Young, G. A. (2023). Splitting strategies for post-selection inference. Biometrika, 110(3), 597–614. doi:10.1093/biomet/asac070

Leiner, J., Duan, B., Wasserman, L. and Ramdas, A. (2023). Data fission: splitting a single data point. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 120(549), 135–146. doi:10.1080/01621459.2023.2270748

Neufeld, A., Dharamshi, A., Gao, L. L. and Witten, D. (2024). Data thinning for convolution-closed distributions. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 25(57), 1–35. https://jmlr.org/papers/v25/23-0446.html

See also

build_tessellation() and get_voronoi_seeds(), which accept this function's result directly as approx_n_cells and n (the first candidate is used, and the output records that it came from here; an NA from it stops them with a note on where it came from); assign_features_to_polygons() and summarize_by_cell() for the steps that follow.

Other resolution: plot.resolution_profile(), resolution_profile(), select_resolution(), summary.resolution_profile()

Examples

library(sf)
set.seed(1)
# Two clearly separated clusters: the elbow should sit near k = 2
pts <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + c(runif(25, 0, 10), runif(25, 90, 100)),
             y = 5e6 + c(runif(25, 0, 10), runif(25, 90, 100))),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
determine_optimal_levels(pts, max_levels = 6)   # 2 1 3: the elbow first
#> [1] 2 1 3
#> attr(,"structured")
#> [1] TRUE
#> attr(,"sag")
#> [1] 3.046636

# Points spread evenly have no elbow: NA, with structured = FALSE and a
# warning of class spatialkit_no_elbow that says why (printed here
# wrapped, in place of the warning)
even <- st_as_sf(data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(200, 0, 100),
                            y = 5e6 + runif(200, 0, 100)),
                 coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
withCallingHandlers(
  determine_optimal_levels(even, max_levels = 6),
  spatialkit_no_elbow = function(w) {
    writeLines(strwrap(conditionMessage(w), 76))
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
#> determine_optimal_levels(): the WSS curve has no elbow: on log-log axes it
#> falls in a straight line, as it does for points with no cluster structure.
#> k = 3 is where the chord rule lands on such a curve, set by the ladder (k =
#> 1 to 6, max_levels) rather than by the data. Choose the count on other
#> grounds, e.g. resolution_profile() with a response. Returning NA
#> (on_no_elbow = "na").
#> [1] NA
#> attr(,"structured")
#> [1] FALSE
#> attr(,"sag")
#> [1] 0
